items.stem: BigQuery on-demand queries are primarily billed based on what?

options.text: The volume of bytes the query scans
options.rationale: Correct: on-demand pricing is based on bytes processed/scanned by the query.
Rows returned do not determine on-demand cost.

options.text: The number of tables in the dataset
options.rationale: Table count does not drive query cost.

options.text: Wall-clock time regardless of data read
options.rationale: On-demand cost tracks bytes scanned, not elapsed time.

items.explanation: Correct: on-demand pricing is based on bytes processed/scanned by the query.

items.stem: Which TWO techniques reduce the bytes a BigQuery query scans? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Partitioning a table and filtering on the partition column
options.rationale: Correct: partition pruning limits the data scanned.

options.text: Selecting only the columns needed instead of SELECT *
options.rationale: Correct: columnar storage means fewer columns scanned means fewer bytes.

options.text: Adding more JOINs to the query
options.rationale: Extra joins generally increase, not reduce, work.

options.text: Returning more rows in the result
options.rationale: Result size does not reduce bytes scanned.

items.explanation: Correct: partition pruning limits the data scanned.

items.stem: What does clustering a BigQuery table do?

options.text: Sorts stored data by the clustering columns to speed selective queries
options.rationale: Correct: clustering co-locates rows by the clustering columns, improving filter/aggregate performance.
Encryption at rest is automatic and unrelated to clustering.
Clustering does not limit row counts.

items.explanation: Correct: clustering co-locates rows by the clustering columns, improving filter/aggregate performance.
